title: A Tiny Motor Inspired by an Ancient Screw
summary:
Scientists have built a tiny motor that spins when electricity runs through it. If they switch the voltage, it spins the other way.

The motor copies an old machine called the Archimedes screw. Long ago, people used it to lift water uphill. It uses a spiral that turns. In the new motor, tiny bits called electrons flow through a spiral molecule. As they flow, they make it turn.

The spiral molecule was made by Prof. Michael Pittelkow's team at the University of Copenhagen. It is only a few millionths of a millimeter big. At the Weizmann Institute in Israel, Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh put molecules between two gold tips. They could stretch or squeeze the tiny screw.

When voltage was added, the molecule turned. Switching the voltage turned it the other way. It is the first motor run by current that is firmly joined to two metal ends and can turn in a direction scientists choose.

Turning brought a surprise. The spinning molecule carried electricity up to 100 times better than when it was still.
why_it_matters: Tiny machines like this could one day power tools far smaller than anything you can see.
